Title: prefers-reduced-motion media query reduces or disables animations
Requirement_Ref: PRD §6.1 — WCAG 2.1 AA motion preferences
Preconditions: Dev server running; browser supports prefers-reduced-motion emulation (Chrome DevTools > Rendering > Emulate CSS media feature)
Test_Steps:
1. Open Chrome DevTools > Rendering panel
2. Set 'Emulate CSS media feature prefers-reduced-motion' to 'reduce'
3. Navigate to http://localhost:3000/
4. Observe the CurriculumMindmap — verify whether ReactFlow animated edges still animate or fall back to static
5. Navigate to /playground and click Play — verify whether NeuralNet framer-motion animations respect the media query
6. Check globals.css for any @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) rules
7. Check CurriculumMindmap.tsx for animated:true on edges — verify if there is a conditional based on reduced-motion
8. Check NeuralNet.tsx for framer-motion variants — verify if motion.div respects prefers-reduced-motion
Test_Data: Media query: prefers-reduced-motion: reduce
Expected_Result: Ideally, all animations (ReactFlow animated edges, framer-motion transitions in NeuralNet, fitView duration) should be reduced or disabled when prefers-reduced-motion is active. However, based on code review: no @media (prefers-reduced-motion) rules exist in globals.css, ReactFlow edges use animated:true unconditionally, and NeuralNet uses framer-motion without useReducedMotion() hook.
Actual_Result: No prefers-reduced-motion support implemented. ReactFlow animated edges continue to animate. Framer-motion animations in NeuralNet continue normally. No CSS or JS conditionals for reduced motion found in the codebase.
Failure_Reason: No prefers-reduced-motion support exists. globals.css has no @media (prefers-reduced-motion) rules. CurriculumMindmap sets animated:true on all edges unconditionally. NeuralNet uses framer-motion without useReducedMotion() hook. Framer-motion does auto-respect the preference for some animations, but the ReactFlow animated edges do not. This fails WCAG 2.1 AA SC 2.3.3 (Animation from Interactions).
Notes: Corrected from previous vague failure. Root cause: animations are unconditionally enabled. Recommendation: add useReducedMotion() from framer-motion and conditionally disable ReactFlow edge animations.

Title: Next.js JavaScript bundle size for initial page load < 200KB (gzipped)
Requirement_Ref: PRD §7.1 — Bundle size budget
Preconditions: Production build (npm run build)
Test_Steps:
1. Run npm run build
2. Examine the build output for First Load JS sizes
3. Record the total First Load JS size for the landing page (/)
4. Record the total First Load JS size for the curriculum page (/curriculum)
5. Record the total First Load JS size for the playground page (/playground)
6. Note the shared chunk sizes
7. Verify each page's First Load JS is < 200KB (gzipped)
8. If any page exceeds 200KB, identify the largest chunks contributing to the bundle
Test_Data: Build command: npm run build; Target: < 200KB gzipped per page
Expected_Result: Each page's First Load JS bundle is under 200KB gzipped. Key dependencies to watch: ReactFlow (@xyflow/react), Three.js (three), framer-motion, d3 — these are large libraries. The transpilePackages: ['three'] in next.config.mjs ensures Three.js is bundled correctly.
Actual_Result: Cannot confirm without running build. The app includes several heavy dependencies: @xyflow/react (ReactFlow), three (Three.js via @react-three/fiber), framer-motion, d3. The landing page loads ReactFlow and the playground loads Three.js components. These libraries are likely to push the First Load JS well over 200KB. However, Next.js code-splitting may keep individual page bundles under budget if libraries are properly tree-shaken.
Failure_Reason: High risk of exceeding 200KB budget based on dependency analysis. The landing page imports @xyflow/react (ReactFlow full bundle ~100KB+ gzipped). The playground imports @react-three/fiber and three (~150KB+ gzipped). Combined with React, Next.js runtime, framer-motion, and d3, the First Load JS for these pages is likely >200KB. Requires actual build to measure. Code-splitting via 'use client' boundaries may help, but ReactFlow and Three.js are inherently large.
Notes: Corrected from previous vague failure. Provided specific dependency analysis. Status remains Fail based on realistic assessment of bundle sizes with ReactFlow + Three.js + framer-motion + d3.

5. Verify the LossSurface3D component either: (a) shows a fallback message, (b) shows a static image, or (c) fails gracefully without crashing the page
6. Verify the rest of the lesson page (MDX text, other components) still renders correctly
7. Check the browser console for error handling (e.g., 'WebGL not available' error message vs unhandled crash)
Test_Data: WebGL: disabled; Components to test: NeuralNet (SVG-based, should work), LossSurface3D (@react-three/fiber, requires WebGL)
Expected_Result: NeuralNet (SVG-based) renders normally without WebGL. LossSurface3D (Three.js/WebGL) fails gracefully — either showing a fallback UI or an error boundary message — without crashing the entire page. Lesson text content remains accessible.
Actual_Result: Code review shows no React error boundary wrapping LossSurface3D or any @react-three/fiber components. If WebGL is unavailable, @react-three/fiber will throw an error that is likely unhandled, potentially crashing the entire lesson page component tree.
Failure_Reason: No graceful degradation implemented for WebGL failure. LossSurface3D is imported directly in [slug]/page.tsx without an error boundary wrapper. @react-three/fiber requires WebGL and will throw if unavailable. No fallback component or try/catch exists around 3D components. The Three.js Canvas component will fail, and without an error boundary, this will crash the entire lesson page.
Notes: Corrected from previous vague failure. Root cause: no Error Boundary component wraps @react-three/fiber components. Recommendation: wrap LossSurface3D (and any Three.js components) in a React error boundary with a static fallback.
